newsitem.title: USA: Summit environmental fight moves to New York.
newsitem.headline: Summit environmental fight moves to New York.

text.p: World leaders who spent the weekend prodding the international economy into shape moved on to an environmental conference in New York on Monday to deal with some of the fall-out from their success.

The Group of Seven major industrial powers and Russia wrapped up a three-day summit in Denver welcoming signs of an improving world economy and committing themselves to spreading the benefits more evenly around the globe.

Although there was concern over Japan's rising trade surplus and a risk of inflation in the United States and Britain, it was essentially a rosy picture, allowing the leaders to focus on other issues, like fighting crime, drugs and diseases.

One of the few contentious areas was the environment, with President Bill Clinton under attack from European countries over U.S. failure to keep its promises over controlling gases that cause the "greenhouse effect".

Under U.S. pressure, the G7 members said they wanted clear and realistic targets for carbon emission cuts but avoided the target -- a 15 percent reduction by the year 2010 -- that the EU has agreed as its position for this week's New York "Earth Summit".
European Commission President Jacques Santer, who attended the G7 meeting, called this disappointing and said: "We must stop the degradation of our climate. The future of the planet is at stake."

The United States accounts for almost a quarter of all greenhouse gases emitted around the world when fossil fuels like oil and coal are burned. Scientists say these emissions could lead to dangerous climate changes in the next century.
The summit communique said the G7 states wanted a "strong agreement" with quantified and legally binding emission targets before a U.N. conference on climate change in Kyoto in December.

Many of the G7 summit leaders were heading national delegations to the week-long New York conference, although Clinton went to California and Russia's President Boris Yeltsin headed for home after the Denver talks.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, for example, was preparing to tell Britons they will have to make fundamental changes in their daily lives to combat global warming, including how they travel, use energy and even what they eat.
"All of us in the United Kingdom -- businesses, consumers, individuals and government -- will need to change our habits, our way of living," Blair was to say in the speech.

He said Britain was taking the lead in Europe on global warming by setting a target of cutting carbon dioxide emissions by 20 percent, from 1990 levels, by 2010. The European Union so far has only agreed to a 15 percent cut.
The New York conference was called to take stock of progress made since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

The most striking result of the Denver summit was the prominent role given to Yeltsin, who was invited to all but one session and placed by Clinton at his right hand at all public appoearances and at the meeting table.

Not all were completely happy that Russia, with its economy in shambles and its democracy in an early and fragile stage, was given a place at the top table in this exclusive and self-appointed club, but all accepted it had happened.

Germany's President Helmut Kohl commented: "One can debate whether Russia has been admitted fully or 90 percent. The fact is that he (Yeltsin) was there, this is the reality and it is a sensible one."
Clinton said at his concluding news conference: "We now feel stronger because we have Russia as a partner."
